courses.title: Rhetoric, Argumnt & Persuasion
courses.course_description: Arguments are a tool we use to build our social realities and the worlds we want to see. In this course, we move beyond “winning debates” to instead ask: How does culture and context convince us what is true, and how do we critically assess those assumptions? Using an interdisciplinary blend of theories and methods from the humanities and social sciences, we will analyze argumentation as a contest over power. We will explore how “common sense” is constructed through discursive repetition and ritual, as well as how media technologies have historically (and in the present) facilitated those constructions. Students will learn to navigate the politics of representation, scrutinize the “mythologies” of Big Tech, and construct arguments that are not only logical, but socially and ethically responsive to the conditions of the world.

courses.title: Ethics of Tech & Communication
courses.course_description: In this course, we will investigate philosophical questions about the nature of technology and communication, as well as ethical questions related to a broad range of specific communication-related technologies. Topics include algorithmic bias and fairness, privacy and surveillance, consent and manipulation, and the environmental impacts of digital technologies. Students will engage with case studies that require applying ethical principles to complex situations.

courses.title: Communicating Science
courses.course_description: This course focuses on strategies for communicating scientific information in professional settings. Students develop a literature review, proposal, and feasibility study; learn how to adapt scientific information to various audiences; and complete exercises on style, grammar, and other elements of effective professional communication. Emphasis on usability, cohesion, and style in each assignment.
